cells.tense: You are here with the pen, meeting what someone else feels without losing where you end.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been making toward someone, and one thing you've been making only for yourself.
cells.core:
You can stand next to what someone is going through without falling into it. You feel the shape of their thing, you stay yourself, and both survive the encounter. The pen is in your hand on this. You aren't managing it — you're doing it, and you know you're doing it.

What you're becoming gets its shape from that contact. Hard to see while it's working, because it doesn't announce itself. The invitation is toward holding this without forcing it: keeping the warmth, letting it stay optional when you need it to be. Some of what you make is for people, and some is only for you, and both are real. Knowing which is which is the next thing.
cells.sheetLine: You feel with people without disappearing into them.
cells.verb: feeling with someone instead of feeling about them
cells.place: in the open where what you are is becoming visible

cells.tense: You are bracing at a version of yourself that other people have not written in yet.
cells.ask: End one thing that's already over, and tell the person involved before the week is out.
cells.core:
You're living inside a future where the other person has caught up, agreed, understood — and the one in front of you is still here, still uncertain, still themselves. The gap gets filled with pressure: sound more certain, explain it again, get them there. The closeness you want is being spent trying to force it.

Underneath, the line between your feeling and theirs has gone thin. A mood arrives in the room and you've already taken it as yours. What's needed isn't a better argument. It's letting one ending be real — clearing something finished so what's next has somewhere to land. One person, one conversation, before the week turns. That's the whole first step.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that closed behind you a long time ago, waiting for it to open.
cells.ask: Say one true small thing about your own day to someone before the day ends.
cells.core:
The people around you feel like they're on the other side of glass: you can see them, you can't feel them, and the surface version of things is what you show. You keep it level, useful, easy. The levelness works. It also keeps the room at a distance you didn't choose.

What's starved isn't the feeling itself — it's your sense of where you actually sit. Reaching for a big emotion on purpose won't get you there; it'll just make you feel broken. Start small: one true thing, said to one actual person, and then notice what it does. Your own true thing first, before you check how it landed.

cells.tense: You are already writing in a room whose pen you believe someone else is holding.
cells.ask: Catch one moment of care you'd normally chalk up to being polite, and say to yourself what it actually was.
cells.core:
People around you feel met. They leave conversations steadier, and they couldn't say exactly why. If asked, you'd say you were just being sensible, keeping things simple, not making it about feelings. The care comes through anyway. That's the strange part. It shapes how you stand next to people without your having signed anything.

You've been treating this as background noise while you look for the real thing. Seeing what's underneath the surface doesn't mean explaining it away. The clearest view is available right now, in the ordinary mechanics of how you treat people. One moment today, with no argument attached, is the whole gesture.
